definition: Because pipeline temperatures aren't constant, unwanted phase changes can occur in transit: in gas pipelines, liquids can condense out and are extremely difficult to remove, while in oil pipelines, gas bubbles can form and damage the pipe.
core_idea: Pipeline engineers must design systems to handle both gas and liquid phases simultaneously because temperature variation along a pipeline can cause the transported fuel to partially change phase, creating operational hazards.
key_points: Gas pipelines: condensed liquids are hard to remove once they form.
Oil pipelines: bubble formation can damage the pipe.
Root cause is non-constant temperature along the pipeline route.
Pipeline design must accommodate both gas and liquid phases of the transported substance.
relationships: A direct consequence of the phase-transition properties described for gases and liquids.
trading_implications: Uncontrolled condensation/bubble formation represents an operational risk to transport infrastructure that can affect delivery reliability and asset integrity.
